extracted.intended_audience: readers or students of classical natural history / natural philosophy (Latin/early-modern scholarship)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and explanatory criteria from a Latin natural-history treatment of animals (De Animalibus, Liber X): causal rules for animal form, behavior, habitat, and adaptation used by the author to classify and explain animal phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immobility of certain marine animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some marine animals (oysters, many conchylia) are immobile because they derive nourishment from the surrounding water and therefore do not need motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual examples: oysters and many shell-animals are fixed to stones; nature makes them hard and fixed because the sea supplies nourishment and motion is unnecessary. The author uses this to explain why many shellfish and sponges are sedentary rather than locomotive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness of shells and corals (cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardness/induration of shells, oysters, and corals is caused by marine conditions: algal growth, saline substances, and the influence of currents that produce durable deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that algae growth and the thick substance created in the sea render shells and corals hard and durable; such hardness often originates during formation so that the organism resists currents and abrasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant-animal resemblance and sensitive plant-parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain trees and plants possess organs or leaves that show animal-like sensitivity or motion (e.g., 'sensitive' leaves that move), blurring plant/animal distinctions in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reports local reports of trees with leaves that behave sensitively or animal-like, and argues that in warm/wet soils some plant-parts may exhibit motion akin to animals; used as evidence that strict plant/animal boundaries are not always observed in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of nourishment source to animal mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: An animal's mode of feeding (feeding from water vs feeding by active foraging) governs its need for motion: animals nourished passively by surrounding medium tend to be less motile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses aquatic examples (sessile mollusks) and terrestrial contrasts to argue that access to distributed nourishment reduces selection pressure for locomotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shells/conchylia formed to resist environmental forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Conchylia and oysters acquire solidity as a protective/adaptive response to marine forces—nature creates firm coverings so they will not be swept away by currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim: fixedness and solidity are not accidents but products of natural advantage—hard shells persist while softer forms would be carried off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine fauna variation explained by local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The diversity and abundance of marine species near shores depend on local food availability, salinity, depth and motion of the water; different water qualities attract or repel different fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples of color changes of water with depth/turbulence (white, green, blue, black) and links these to differing fish distributions; also cites geographic differences across seas and coasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations of fishes and aquatic animals (limbs/pediculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fishes show limb-like appendages or foot-like forms (various local reports of fishes with 'pedes' or limb-like structures), explained as adaptations to specific habitats (e.g., to rest on shore, crawl, or resist currents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author records reports of bipedal or multi-limbed fishes and treats them as providential adaptations for particular ways of life (holding to rocks, moving in shallow waters, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in animal intelligence and tameness by class
rubrics_metrics.description: Different animal classes (fish, birds, quadrupeds) have characteristic intellect and tameness: e.g., many fish are dull and untamable, but dolphins are intelligent and can be tamed; some birds are tame while others are wild.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational guidance: the author contrasts species (delphini as clever and compassionate; many small fish as dull) and notes that tameness often correlates with temperament and ecological niche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of reproductive ease with brevity and 'lowness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Species that are easily generated and multiply rapidly tend to be of lower nobility and shorter duration (e.g., small, prolific animals perish quickly and are less 'noble').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues a general law: facile generation implies easy destruction; thus high fecundity is associated with small size and rapid turnover (examples: numerous small island species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet-based classification of animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals are classifiable by their diet into groups such as herbivores (fruit-eating), carnivores, omnivores, and those sustained by humic/elemental substances; diet shapes form and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text enumerates 'quatuor modis' and gives examples (elephants and many mammals eating fruits, others feeding on herbs or mixed diets) and relates diet to size, habitat and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental temperature and humidity determine size/form
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate (heat, cold, dryness, humidity) influences animal size and constitution: cold regions tend to produce smaller animals similar to rustic forms; warm and humid zones favor larger forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Indians (warm region) produce small, dry animals adapted to scarcity of water; temperate vs frigid comparisons given for rabbits, mice, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical adaptations for flight in birds
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds' small heads and beaks, lightweight bodies, special digestive organs (e.g., two stomachs/crops or gizzards) and reduced feet are adaptations that enable flight by reducing weight and aiding digestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains causally: small head reduces weight and the need for large jaws; a second stomach/grinding organ substitutes for the lack of mastication; leg reduction lightens the body for aerial life. Variations (dental aberrations in some birds) are considered varieties rather than perfection failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small head and small beak advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: A small head (and correspondingly small beak) is advantageous for birds because it reduces weight, aids in flight, allows for lighter plumage and better vision from height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists multiple benefits: lighter weight for flying, enabling fine plumage and powerful sight; when an avian species deviates (aberrant forms) it may still be viable but represents variety rather than perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coloration and display as functional/variable traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Feather coloration and ornamental traits (e.g., peacock's tail) serve display functions and are subject to physiological changes (e.g., pallor or reddening due to blood/expansion) and seasonal or emotional variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peacock example: plumage coloration can change with blood/expansion; the author notes both permanent ornamental selection and transient color changes tied to physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nest placement and anti-predator architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Some birds deliberately place nests in thorny or otherwise protected trees, build long, narrow nests with one approach, or collect excrement to obstruct access—adaptive behaviors minimizing predation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a small passerine whose nesting behavior (thorny trees, narrow access) protects eggs/pullets and discourages predators; details include nest length and use of thorn barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic color diagnostics (water color indicates depth and current)
rubrics_metrics.description: The color and appearance of water (white, green, blue, black, argent) vary with depth, motion, and bottom composition; these visible qualities indicate different marine conditions and associated fauna.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: shallow sand yields white; medium depth green; deep moving waters blue; argentine tint near still basins. The author links these appearances with wind and mountain shadow effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterranean animal morphology (mole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals living permanently underground (moles) show morphological specializations: small/hidden eyes, extreme aversion to air/light, short limbs, very sharp digging claws and shortened tails appropriate to burrowing life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses mole anatomy to argue causal adaptation to subterranean life: eye reduction, limb shortening, claw sharpness for digging, and behavioral intolerance of exposure to light and air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in pulses and respiratory signs among species
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulse and respiration differ among species in ways that do not always parallel human physiology (e.g., pulses in some animals are in different members or manifest differently), so one should not uncritically apply human norms to other animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states that pulse/respiration manifestations vary (citing dogs, goats, etc.) and that certain commonly asserted homologies (Aristotle/Galenic disputes) may not be universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of environmental air quality with bird abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: Regions with purer air and abundant food support greater numbers and varieties of birds; abundance of birds indicates good air and ample sustenance in a region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used diagnostically: when many birds are present (especially of multiple species), it suggests the air is healthy and the environment supports life; the author cautions, however, that local topography must be considered (valleys vs hills).
